statement: A business is not an insurer against random third-party crime. Customer status matters, but guard/security duty needs a foreseeability trigger such as prior similar incidents, created risk, imminent danger, or comparable notice.
trigger: A customer is attacked by an unknown third party and sues for missing security guards.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 344 cmt. f; Restatement (Second) of Torts § 314A business-invitee principles, lawyer-confirmation only.

statement: Lock the exact duty before reading the choices: the question is not whether Esther was a customer, but whether these facts triggered a guard-duty against a random third-party attack.
trigger: A choice says duty exists merely because the plaintiff bought or completed something at the business.

statement: For prescription products, an adequate warning to the prescribing healthcare provider can satisfy the manufacturer's warning duty; the manufacturer is not automatically required to warn the patient directly.
trigger: Prescription-only product + professional warning to prescriber + jurisdiction follows learned-intermediary rule.
authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability § 6(d); learned-intermediary case law.

statement: On a failure-to-warn call, an answer saying the warned-of risk happened proves injury, not warning defect.
trigger: Choice points to injury by the described risk instead of the adequacy or audience of the warning.

statement: Negligent entrustment looks to control or supply of the chattel plus known unsafe use; formal legal title is not the gate.
trigger: Defendant is not owner but has key, permission authority, or control and hands the chattel to an impaired or inexperienced user.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 308, 390; Delana v. CED Sales, Inc.

statement: Lock the target defendant first: the call asks about Lydia's duty, so an answer focused only on Barnabas's operation is adjacent-call bait.
trigger: The injured plaintiff sues the person who handed over the chattel, not the person who physically used it.

statement: For negligent misrepresentation by a professional information supplier, economic-loss duty is limited to a known person or limited group for a specific transaction or substantially similar transaction. It does not run to every foreseeable later reader.
trigger: professional report, economic loss, unknown third-party reader
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 552; Bily v. Arthur Young & Co.; Ultramares Corp. v. Touche.

statement: When one finalist says 'foreseeable reader' and another says 'known or limited class for a transaction,' name the axis as targeted-use duty, not general foreseeability.
trigger: unknown later reader relying on a client-republished report

statement: Public-concern false light points to actual malice: the publisher knew the false implication was false or recklessly disregarded that risk. Strict liability is the trap.
trigger: false-light claim + public-concern publication + pre-publication contradiction
authority: Time, Inc. v. Hill, 385 U.S. 374 (1967); New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964)

statement: On a mental-state call, cut choices that describe harm, remedy, tort category, or no-fault liability before judging doctrine.
trigger: call asks 'what mental-state showing'

statement: A later safety fix is not proof that the earlier condition was negligent. Its limited use is a non-breach purpose such as feasibility, and only if that purpose is genuinely disputed.
trigger: Defendant changes the condition after the injury.
authority: Fed. R. Evid. 407; Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §3.

statement: Lock the call to use, not hindsight. First cut the two extremes: later fix proves everything, later fix proves nothing.
trigger: A post-injury safety change appears in a breach question.

statement: Res ipsa is an inference bridge. It can apply when the plaintiff lacks direct proof of the exact defect, and it permits but does not compel a negligence finding.
trigger: The call asks whether res ipsa is available and the stem says the plaintiff lacks direct defect proof.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 328D

statement: Contractor involvement does not automatically erase res ipsa responsibility when the defendant retained operational responsibility for the instrumentality.
trigger: The stem says a contractor serviced the mechanism but the defendant retained operational responsibility and received reports.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 328D responsibility/control formulation

statement: Cut the absolute contractor and automatic-judgment answers first. Then resolve the residual pair by asking whether the missing exact defect is fatal or is the reason res ipsa matters.
trigger: One answer says no exact defect, one says inference without exact defect.

statement: Strict products liability for a defective product is aimed at commercial sellers or distributors, not a person who merely uses the product.
trigger: The defendant is using, testing, or operating a product rather than selling or distributing it.
authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability § 1.

statement: Cause and status are not enough; the plaintiff’s argument must supply negligence, intent, or a strict-liability category. Unreasonable conduct supplies the negligence route.
trigger: A best-argument call with choices that name cause, status, or product defect.
authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 3.

statement: On a best-argument call, pick the answer that gives the plaintiff a legal route to liability; do not require the answer to prove the whole case.
trigger: The call asks for the claimant’s most effective argument.

statement: Plaintiff-side insurance is collateral. A negligence defendant gets no credit for benefits paid by the plaintiff's own insurer; credit is for payments by the defendant, someone acting for the defendant, or another actor subject to the same tort liability.
trigger: Defendant asks to reduce a tort award because plaintiff's own insurer already paid.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 920A.

statement: For setoff questions, ask who paid and whose liability the payer was tied to before reacting to double-recovery language.
trigger: Motion to reduce damages after insurance or settlement payment.

statement: For a business invitee, owner liability turns on dangerous conditions the owner knew about or would discover by reasonable care, plus failure to protect.
trigger: public-facing business premises plus customer injury from a condition on the premises
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 332, 343

statement: A product defect alone points to strict products liability only when the defendant is in the business of selling that type of product.
trigger: injury from a defective component but defendant is sued as premises owner
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A

statement: Lock the named defendant before reading the added facts: the winning fact must create liability for Lydia, not for Barnabas or the product chain.
trigger: one defendant named in the call, but choices mention product defect, contractor conduct, and customer payment

statement: Danger invites rescue: when a person negligently creates apparent human peril, even to himself, a reasonable rescue attempt is foreseeable and the rescuer may recover for rescue injuries caused by that negligence.
trigger: rescuer injured while trying to save someone from danger the defendant negligently created
authority: Wagner v. International Railway Co., 232 N.Y. 176 (1921); self-peril applications recognized in later rescue-doctrine cases.

statement: In a party-result answer set, test the because-clause before choosing the winner. A correct party with a wrong reason is still out.
trigger: choices split between plaintiff/defendant and each uses 'because'

statement: Appropriation is not limited to exact name or photograph. A clearly recognizable, unauthorized commercial evocation of the plaintiff’s identity can be enough.
trigger: Ad uses a lookalike, soundalike, persona, or identity cues to sell a product.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 652C; Midler v. Ford Motor Co., 849 F.2d 460 (9th Cir. 1988).

statement: For appropriation calls, sort the array by the three trigger facts: identity use, commercial advantage, and no consent. Extra requirements like exact name/photo, insult, or false fact are trap add-ons.
trigger: One answer mirrors identity-use facts while others add conditions.

statement: Rescue doctrine needs a negligent peril-maker. A rescuer's injury is charged to the person whose negligence created the peril, not merely to the person who needed help.
trigger: rescuer sues the imperiled person's estate
authority: Wagner v. International Railway, 232 N.Y. 176, 133 N.E. 437 (N.Y. 1921); Cornell Wex rescue doctrine

statement: Lock the target actor before judging the rescue. If the rescuer sues the imperiled person's estate, ask what that imperiled person did wrong.
trigger: choices discuss the rescuer's reasonableness, public policy, or failed benefit

statement: False light needs publicity to the public or a broad audience. A private one-listener accusation is not enough, even if it is false.
trigger: false light claim + one private listener + no repeat
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §652E; Restatement publicity commentary.

statement: Commercial use of a person's identity is appropriation, not false light. Do not borrow the neighboring privacy tort's element.
trigger: false light choice using identity, likeness, or commercial use
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §652C and §652E.

statement: When two answers say No, keep the No reason that matches the stem's decisive fact. Here, private audience beats commercial-use vocabulary.
trigger: two No choices in a privacy-tort element question

statement: Negligence turns on unreasonable conduct in light of a foreseeable risk. A fact that makes the specific risk not foreseeable can defeat breach.
trigger: The added fact says the missing safety device is usually present.
authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 3; negligence factors include foreseeable likelihood/severity and burden of precautions.

statement: Contributory negligence requires negligent plaintiff conduct that contributed to the harm. A fact that the plaintiff would have avoided injury by doing something else is not enough by itself.
trigger: The answer says the plaintiff would not have been hurt from another position.
authority: Common-law contributory negligence rule; see Cornell Wex summary.

statement: In an added-fact defense question, sort each option by what it attacks: defendant breach, plaintiff negligence, other cause, or other party. The best defense fact usually attacks an element of the plaintiff's claim against this defendant.
trigger: Choices point in four different blame directions.

statement: In malpractice, proof that the doctor broke a professional rule is not enough; the plaintiff must prove that the broken rule caused the injury.
trigger: Stem gives standard-of-care evidence but no evidence the missed consult would change the outcome.
authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts §§ 26, 29; medical-malpractice causation doctrine.

statement: When the alleged tort creates the condition requiring life support, later withdrawal of support normally does not cut off causation.
trigger: Family/court withdraws support after the medical injury creates a permanent vegetative state.
authority: State v. Pelham; State v. Patterson.

statement: Track the alleged breach, not the whole medical timeline. The question is not procedure-to-death; it is missed-consult-to-injury.
trigger: One answer proves breach while another says no evidence the omitted consult would change the outcome.

statement: For negligent misrepresentation by a professional information supplier, no contract privity is required when the plaintiff is the known person, or one of a limited known group, expected to rely on the information in the transaction.
trigger: professional report + named recipient or limited known group + business reliance
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §552; Private Mortgage Investment Services, Inc. v. Hotel & Club Associates, Inc.

statement: When the array swings from no contract to every foreseeable reader, bracket both extremes and look for the named-recipient middle lane.
trigger: choices include no contract, every foreseeable, and named-recipient reliance

statement: Strict liability for an abnormally dangerous activity follows the special danger, not every accident near the activity. The injury must be the kind of harm that made the activity abnormal.
trigger: The stem gives an abnormally dangerous activity plus an ordinary injury mechanism.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §519(2)

statement: In a 2-yes / 2-no strict-liability array, do not pick the outcome first. Pick the reason that links this injury to the risk named in the answer.
trigger: Two answers say yes, two say no, and only one answer talks about the injury source.

statement: Battery intent points at harmful/offensive contact or apprehension of that contact. It does not require intent to injure, appreciation of risk, or bad motive; a child can be liable if the child formed that contact-level intent.
trigger: Battery call plus choices that talk about injury, risk, age, or anger.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 13, 18; Garratt v. Dailey.

statement: When the answer array gives four mental states, choose the one aimed at the tort named in the call. For battery, the contact-target answer beats injury, risk, and motive answers.
trigger: Battery call with choices about contact, injury, risk, and anger.

statement: When a jurisdiction recognizes negligent erroneous death notice, the claim does not fail merely because the plaintiff was outside physical danger or because the reported death was false.
trigger: False death notice to close family + severe distress + jurisdiction recognizes the category.
authority: Johnson v. State of New York, 37 N.Y.2d 378 (1975); Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 47(b).

statement: When the stem says the jurisdiction recognizes a special category, cut choices that answer the ordinary default lane instead of the special lane.
trigger: Stem phrase: jurisdiction recognizes negligent erroneous death notice as a special NIED category.

statement: In nuisance remedies, a court can tailor abatement to a reasonable fix. Avoidable-consequences principles can limit damages, but they do not erase the nuisance or require total closure.
trigger: The stem gives both a substantial interference and a moderate-cost abatement option.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 822, 826; Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co., 26 N.Y.2d 219 (1970).

statement: When the choices are shutdown, no remedy, punitive-only, and tailored abatement, treat the first three as remedy oversteers. Match the remedy to the stem’s reasonable-fix fact.
trigger: The stem says a moderate-cost change would end nearly all interference.

statement: For negligence by an active operator, the foreseeability target is the plaintiff/class/risk created by the defendant's conduct, not the exact prior event that put the plaintiff there and not whether the defendant's own careless act was foreseeable.
trigger: answer choices all complete 'foreseeable that ___'
authority: Palsgraf v. Long Island R.R.; Restatement (Third) of Torts §§ 7, 29

statement: When every choice starts from 'foreseeable that,' compare the object of foreseeability first. Set-stage cause, exact chain, defendant breach, and plaintiff risk are different targets.
trigger: same grammatical stem repeated across all choices

statement: A statutory or otherwise nondelegable safety duty stays with the hirer even when the negligent work is done by an independent contractor.
trigger: statutory/public safety duty plus outside contractor
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 409, 424

statement: When the stem gives a legal safety duty and an outside contractor, do not choose the all-or-nothing contractor answers; look for the duty-stays-with-the-hirer route.
trigger: statutory duty + hired contractor + injured public entrant
